title: Come with me if you want massive arms (Step by Step MASSterplan)
summary: A practical six-step arm training plan split into novice, intermediate and advanced stages based on arm-isolation experience, not strength. It starts with one biceps and one long-head triceps movement for 3-6 weekly sets and adds movements, sets and frequency only when progression stalls, keeping weight on the bar as the main driver.
claims: Doing 15 push-ups teaches more than reading a whole book about push-ups; practice beats theory
Chin-ups for biceps and bench for triceps produce bodybuilders with small arms; big arms come from isolation
He built 18-inch arms naturally through isolation, not compounds
The novice/intermediate/advanced stages refer to arm-isolation experience, not strength: a 600 lb deadlifter can be a novice at arm training
Step 1 (novice): pick only one biceps movement and one long-head triceps movement; a lateral-head isolation is optional since presses already hit it
Pick the arm movement you enjoy and can do comfortably, not the trendy one; trying several curls before settling on one is fine, but then stick to it
For novices favour less strict, intense isolation movements (standing dumbbell curls, lying triceps extensions) over precise ones like slow-tempo 45-degree cable extensions; precision comes later
Step 2 (novice): 3-6 sets per week per muscle, either 3 sets once a week or 3 sets twice a week; never 6 sets at once since novices lack the endurance
Novice arm rep range: 6-10 or 8-12 reps with proper form; 20-25 rep sets are pump garbage
Novice arms are spaghetti and respond to anything; 9 sets instead of 6 might give marginally more but risks exceeding poor recovery and work capacity
Start with minimal volume to keep volume increases as a gear in reserve for later; doing too much early leaves nothing to progress with
With so few sets every set must be pushed to absolute failure
Bro arm training (around 20 sets each for biceps and triceps weekly, 40 total) produces no gains because it is junk volume
Arm isolation does not interfere with compounds: three sets of curls on Wednesday will not hurt Friday chin-ups; only avoid double dipping such as curls right before chin-ups
If you add lateral-head triceps isolation, place it far from presses (e.g. isolation Monday, presses Thursday) or, if on the same day, do the compound first
Novices told they can progress with sets and reps hyper-focus on pump and volume and stop adding weight, going in circles for a year with no arm growth
Keeping novices at 3-6 sets forces the only progression route to be adding weight to the bar
Each step can last 6 months to 2 years; stay a novice as long as you keep progressing, and only move on when you plateau
Arms are not legs: use small jumps of 2.5-5 lb or 10 lb (5 per side), and if a weight increase pushes you below the rep range, go back down
Do not ego lift curls; whatever weight brings you to failure in 6-10 reps is the relevant weight
Step 3 (intermediate): add one more movement per muscle, different from the first, for 2 biceps and 2-3 triceps movements total
For triceps a ratio of two long-head movements to one lateral-head movement (which can be a triceps-biased press) works well; three long-head ones overdoes it
Step 4 (intermediate): build up gradually toward 6-12 weekly sets per muscle, adding a couple of sets at a time only when needed; 12 is the cap
Do no more than 2-4 arm sets per muscle per session; e.g. 10 biceps sets as 4 of the first movement plus 3 and 3 of the second
Intermediate rep ranges: a strict movement at 6-10 and the other at 8-12, never below 6 and up to 15; a triceps-biased press like close-grip bench can stay at 3-6 or 6-10
Whether you do 6 or 8 sets matters little; what matters is doing the sets for real within the guidelines
Intermediates stall because they use all their gears at once and fall for the volume meme, curling the same weight in December and July
Avoid lifting ADHD: rotating many variations for novelty satisfies the brain and kills progression; stick to two variations

Soft variations (same movement, different implement, e.g. dumbbell to cable curl, towel or rope) are unlimited because they do not cost progression; switching preacher curl to cheat barbell curl is a real variation
Step 5 (advanced): add one very strict movement per muscle, like preacher curls or a triceps machine, and rotate (e.g. two movements week A, two week B) among three favourites
He only uses three biceps movements: standing curls, preacher curls and EZ-bar curls
At high arm volume the main risks are elbow/tendon injuries and loss of motivation; rotations help with both
For arms you keep adding weight, then add reps and sets until you can add weight again, then drop back down in sets (the 85% rule)
Step 6 (advanced): still only 6-15 weekly sets, but train arms whenever you have recovery available; he trains biceps and triceps every two days or more
The full plan takes years; as a natural you must treat arm training as a serious business
He made insane arm gains in three months by refining the process rather than adding anything new
